newsitem.title: USA: Sun aims to boost Latam business.
newsitem.headline: Sun aims to boost Latam business.

text.p: Sun Microsystems expects its business in Latin America to quadruple over the next few years, from its current annual sales there of about $100 million annually, said Mike Kelley, regional director - Interamerica for Sun Microsystems Computer Company Tuesday.
"We plan to quadruple that in the next three or four years," he told Reuters in an interview.

Currently, only about 1-1/2 percent of Sun's business comes from Latin America, compared with the three percent that is typical for the U.S. computer industry. The company said it is the leader in the Latin American Unix workstation market.

Sun has offices in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Venezuela and has established country distributors in the rest of the region, having tripled its investment and head count there since 1993.

But the company, known for its powerful UNIX-based desktop workstations, is only about a dozen years old itself and has only been in Latin America for the past four or five years, working to establish itself there, Kelley said.
"In some countries, it's been an uphill battle," he said. In most cases, Sun's workstations have replaced International Business Machines Corp mainframes installed in Latin America.
"UNIX vendors have not had much of a presence," Kelley said, noting that Sun had to make its identity known as a company, and promote Unix "as a credible computing environment."

Kelley said he expected computer firms' business in Latin America to rise even higher before too long, as the market there expands. Currently, spending on information technology in Latin America is 0.4 percent of Gross Domestic Product, half the world average of 0.8 percent. In the United States, such spending totals 1.1 percent of GDP.

Keys to successful computer marketing in Latin America include being flexible in ways that might not be required in the United States. For example, a dealer in Venezuela that had sold Sun products for years went bankrupt and the company was able to put together its own sales team "literally over a weekend," Kelley said. "...Sun is flexible when things like that happen."

Kelley said Sun views Latin America as a particularly ripe market for Java, a computer programming language that Sun introduced in mid-1995 that has captured the attention of the industry for its ability operate across virtually all computer systems in a relatively secure manner.

In the region, more than half of investment in technology is for single-user systems, making Java a natural fit because it would allow software to be shared "on demand" by different types of systems linked on a network.
